blocks.x: Core definitions
Enzyme A specialised catalyst, mainly protein (and occasionally RNA), that mediates virtually all of the thousands of metabolic reactions occurring rapidly in cells.
Substrate The substance upon which an enzyme acts; enzymes are highly selective (specific) about the substrates they bind and the reactions they catalyse.

Cofactor / Coenzyme A nonprotein component — a metal ion or organic molecule (coenzyme) — required by some enzymes for catalytic function; many coenzymes are vitamins or contain vitamins in their structure.

Enzymes acting in series form metabolic pathways: nutrients are degraded, energy released is captured in useful forms, and precursors are generated to build the cell's thousands of biomolecules — all while regulatory enzymes sense and respond to the cell's momentary needs.
Substrate + Enzyme→ Enzyme–Substrate Complex→ Product + Enzyme (regenerated)
Glucose: thermodynamic potentiality

Glucose can sit on a shelf indefinitely, yet its oxidation to CO₂ and H₂O releases ΔG° = -2,870 kJ/mol — a large, exergonic amount of energy. The reaction simply does not occur under normal conditions without a catalyst. Enzymes lower the free energy of activation (ΔG‡), letting thermodynamically favourable reactions like this proceed at extraordinarily rapid rates in the cell.
Catalytic power, specificity & naming
Three defining qualities — catalytic power, specificity and regulation — set enzymes apart from ordinary catalysts, and a systematic naming scheme organises the thousands of enzymes cells use.
Rate accelerations up to 10¹⁶ over uncatalysed levels, achieved in dilute aqueous solution under mild temperature and pH.
No substrate is diverted to side reactions; no wasteful by-products form. Recognition is via structural complementarity at the active site.
Achieved from controlling how much enzyme protein a cell makes to rapid, reversible interactions with inhibitors and activators.
The enzyme–substrate cycle

Substrates bind at the enzyme's active site to form an enzyme–substrate complex. The enzyme converts substrate to product, releases it, and is regenerated unchanged — free to bind another substrate molecule.
Naming enzymes

blocks.title: From trivial names to systematic classification

blocks.x: Traditionally, enzymes were named by adding the suffix -ase to the substrate they acted on — urease for the urea-hydrolysing enzyme, phosphatase for enzymes hydrolysing phosphoryl groups. Others acquired names bearing little resemblance to their activity: catalase (peroxide-decomposing), and the proteases trypsin and pepsin.

Because of the confusion these trivial names caused, an International Commission on Enzymes was established in 1956 to create a systematic basis for enzyme nomenclature. Enzymes are now classified and formally named by the reaction they catalyse. A series of four numbers (class, subclass, sub-subclass, entry) specifies each enzyme — e.g. chymotrypsin is EC 3.4.21.1 and trypsin is EC 3.4.21.4.
Seven classes of enzyme-catalysed reactions

c: Oxidation reactions; transfer of electrons from one molecule to another
Catalyse the transfer of groups of atoms from one molecule to another
Hydrolysis reactions; cleavage of substrates by water
Addition of groups to double bonds, or formation of double bonds via removal of groups
Transfer of groups from one position to another on the same molecule
Catalyse the joining of two molecules to form a new bond
Catalyse the movement of ions or molecules across membranes, or their separation within membranes
Ubiquinone reductase, ATP synthase, ascorbate ferrireductase

blocks.x: Cofactors, prosthetic groups & the B-vitamins
Some enzymes catalyse using protein structure alone; many others need nonprotein cofactors — metal ions or coenzymes — and a surprising number of coenzymes are built directly from dietary vitamins.

Prosthetic group A coenzyme so tightly (sometimes covalently) bound to its enzyme that it is difficult to separate. The active protein–prosthetic group complex is the holoenzyme; the protein alone, without the prosthetic group, is the apoenzyme.
Why vitamins?

Vitamins are required in the diet because the organism either cannot synthesise them, or its rate of usage exceeds its rate of synthesis. They fall into two solubility classes: water-soluble (Vitamin B group, Vitamin C) and fat-soluble (Vitamins A, D, E, K).

NAD/NADP and the flavin coenzymes

items: NAD and NADP act as soluble electron carriers between proteins — substrates for enzymes involved in redox reactions.
NAD (NADH) is primarily involved in catabolic reactions; NADPH (reduced NADP) is primarily involved in biosynthetic reactions.
In most cells, NAD levels are much higher than NADH, while NADPH levels are much higher than NADP — matching their catabolic/biosynthetic roles.
Reaction: NAD⁺ + 2e⁻ (+2H⁺) → NADH₂ (each hydrogen atom transferred as H⁺ + e⁻).
Riboflavin is the precursor to the flavin coenzymes FMN and FAD. Flavins are yellow and light-sensitive; riboflavin deficiency is rare.
FMN and FAD are non-covalently attached to their enzymes but generally do not dissociate — they are prosthetic groups that act as storage locations for electrons within the protein.
The functional part is the isoalloxazine ring, which accepts or transfers electrons one at a time (fully oxidised → partially reduced → fully reduced), though it can carry up to two.

blocks.x: Metal ions, coenzymes & the enzymes that use them
Rates, equations & reaction conditions
Kinetics — the study of reaction rates — reveals an enzyme's maximum velocity, its binding affinities, and how pH and temperature shape its activity. This knowledge underlies rational drug design.
The Michaelis-Menten equation

items: Lenore Michaelis and Maud Leonora Menten proposed that enzyme (E) and substrate (S) associate reversibly to form an enzyme–substrate complex (ES): E + S ⇌ ES, at rapid equilibrium.
Product (P) forms in a second step as ES dissociates: E + S ⇌ ES → E + P. The enzyme is then free to bind another substrate molecule.
The Michaelis constant, Km = (k₋₁ + k₂)/k₁, substituted into the rate expression gives the Michaelis-Menten equation: v = Vmax[S] / ([S] + Km).

The rate v at any time is set by two constants — Km and Vmax — and the substrate concentration [S]. As [S] rises, v approaches Vmax (the plot rises then plateaus, forming the classic saturation curve).

blocks.x: Enzyme units & turnover number
The amount of enzyme that catalyses 1 μmol of product formation per minute. Assay conditions (pH, ionic strength, temperature) must be specified since enzymes are sensitive to all three.
The amount of enzyme catalysing conversion of 1 mol of substrate per second. 1 katal = 6 × 10⁷ IU.

kcat measures an enzyme's maximal catalytic activity — substrate molecules converted to product per enzyme molecule per unit time at saturating [S] (also called molecular activity). At saturating [S], k₂ = Vmax/[Eт] = kcat.
Catalase40M/s
Lysozyme0.5/s
Catalase has the highest known turnover number (40 million H₂O₂ molecules/sec); lysozyme, at the other extreme, needs 2 seconds to cleave one glycosidic bond.
Effect of pH on enzymatic activity

Enzyme–substrate recognition and catalysis are greatly pH-dependent: ionisable side chains and prosthetic groups shape secondary/tertiary structure and the active site, while ionising groups on the substrate affect binding. Enzymes are active only over a limited pH range, each with a particular optimum.
Effect of temperature on enzymatic activity

Like most chemical reactions, enzyme-catalysed rates generally increase with rising temperature — most reactions double in rate for every 10°C rise (Q₁₀ = 2, the ratio of activities at two temperatures 10°C apart) if the enzyme is stable and fully active.

However, above 50–60°C most enzymes decline in activity: rising rate is offset by thermal denaturation of protein structure. Not all enzymes are thermally labile — enzymes of the thermophilic bacterium Thermus aquaticus, found in hot springs, retain full activity above 90°C.
Perturbing, specifying & controlling enzyme action

Systematic perturbations — inhibitors — reveal how enzymes work. Meanwhile, cells fine-tune enzymatic activity through specificity models, feedback, gene control, covalent modification, allostery, zymogens and isoenzymes.
Competitive, noncompetitive & uncompetitive
Competitive reversible
Substrate and inhibitor compete for the same active site. High [S] overcomes the inhibitor's effect.
Noncompetitive reversible
Inhibitor binds an allosteric site, reducing enzyme efficacy. Cannot be overcome by raising [S].
Uncompetitive reversible
Inhibitor binds only the enzyme–substrate complex, not the free enzyme, at neither active nor allosteric site.
Covalent, stable, and mechanism-based

items: Irreversible inhibitors cause stable, covalent alterations in enzymes, decreasing the concentration of active enzyme. The kinetic pattern resembles noncompetitive inhibition, but reaction with E (and ES) is not instantaneous — activity falls off over time as E + I → EI proceeds. Unlike reversible inhibition, dilution or dialysis does not dissociate the EI complex.

Suicide substrates (mechanism-based inactivators) are inhibitory substrate analogues that generate a very reactive group via regular enzyme action; this group forms a covalent bond within the active site, causing irreversible inhibition and labelling a critical functional group.

Penicillin covalently reacts with serine residues in the active site of glycoprotein peptidase (which cross-links bacterial peptidoglycan), blocking cell wall synthesis and leaving bacteria vulnerable to osmotic lysis.
Eflornithine, a drug for sleeping sickness, is a suicide inhibitor of ornithine decarboxylase.

blocks.x: Lock-and-key vs. induced fit
The enzyme resembles a rigid "lock" and its substrate the "key." Captures specificity, but enzymes are not rigid templates.

Enzymes are flexible, conformationally dynamic molecules. Substrate binding is an interactive process — the active site's shape is modified upon binding (as seen when hexokinase's active-site cleft closes around glucose, creating a solvent-inaccessible lining).
Controls over enzymatic activity

items: 1Product build-up: rate slows as equilibrium ([P]/[S] = Keq) is approached; some enzymes are inhibited by their own products (feedback inhibition).
2Substrate & cofactor availability: rate rises with [S] until enzyme saturation; Km values approximate in vivo substrate concentrations.
3Genetic control: induction (activating synthesis) and repression (shutting it down) change enzyme amounts — minutes in bacteria, hours or longer in eukaryotes.
4Covalent modification: reversible attachment of a group (e.g. a phosphoryl moiety via protein kinase, removed by protein phosphatase) switches enzymes active/inactive.
5Allosteric regulation: noncovalent binding of small-molecule effectors (activators/inhibitors) at a site other than the active site, giving a near-instantaneous cellular response.

blocks.x: Zymogens, isoenzymes & modulator proteins

Some proteins are synthesised as inactive precursors (zymogens/proenzymes) that gain full activity only upon specific, irreversible proteolytic cleavage. Insulin is generated by excising a peptide from proinsulin.

Blood clotting is driven by a cascade of zymogen activations — an amplification that allows rapid clotting after injury. Seven active clotting factors are serine proteases (kallikrein, XIIa, XIa, IXa, VIIa, Xa, thrombin), triggered via intrinsic (abnormal surfaces) or extrinsic (tissue-released factors) pathways.

Several enzymes exist in more than one quaternary form — structurally equivalent but catalytically distinct subunits. Mammalian lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) exists as five isozymes from tetrameric combinations of subunits A and B: A4, A3B, A2B2, AB3, B4. Isozymes differ in substrate affinity and product-inhibition sensitivity, and different tissues (liver, muscle, heart, kidney, brain) express different proportions as appropriate to their metabolic needs.

Modulator proteins bind to enzymes and influence their activity. cAMP-dependent protein kinase exists as dimers of catalytic and regulatory subunits; dissociation of the regulatory (modulator) subunits activates the catalytic subunits, while reassociation suppresses activity. Phosphoprotein phosphatase inhibitor-1 (PPI-1), when phosphorylated, binds to and inhibits phosphoprotein phosphatase.
